newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE - Pro-business Sharif tipped to win Pakistan polls.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Pro-business Sharif tipped to win Pakistan polls.

text.p: Nawaz Sharif vows to revive the economy, tackle corruption and restore Pakistan's tarnished reputation if, as many expect, he wins the February 3 election.

"Pakistan needs now to project a new image in the world," he told Reuters in a recent interview. "We have become a laughing stock where every time the president and prime minister are fighting one another. This must now come to an end."
Sharif, an industrialist, served as prime minister from 1990 to 1993, when he was dismissed by a former president, restored by the Supreme Court and then manoeuvred into resigning.

His government did much to liberalise Pakistan's regulated economy and privatise state-run industries, but spent heavily on costly projects such as the yellow taxi scheme whereby duty-free imported cars were to be sold on easy terms to the unemployed.
Sharif's new chance for power follows the downfall of his main rival, Benazir Bhutto, sacked by President Farooq Leghari on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
The charges were strikingly similar to those cited by then president Ghulam Ishaq Khan when he removed Sharif.

Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) appears weakened by allegations of sleaze that marked its three years in office and by a challenge from a splinter PPP group led by Ghinwa Bhutto, Lebanese-born widow of Benazir's murdered brother Murtaza.
Sharif exudes quiet confidence in the outcome of the polls, brushing aside suggestions that charismatic former cricketer turned politician Imran Khan might eat into his vote bank.
"He (Imran) has yet to establish his credentials in politics. Politics is completely different from cricket," said Sharif, a passionate follower of Pakistan's best-loved sport.

His Pakistan Muslim League (PML), with strong support in urban areas, especially his home city of Lahore, believes it is poised for triumph at the polls, but questions hang over how much real power it will be able to exercise in government.

He denies widespread speculation in the local media that he has reached secret understandings with Leghari, the military or the caretakers on how a future PML government would rule, in exchange for being allowed a clear run at the elections.

Leghari and his handpicked caretaker government launched an anti-corruption drive after sacking Bhutto, but have barred few major politicians from either party -- although Bhutto's jailed husband Asif Ali Zardari ruled himself out of the race.
The president says he is keen to ensure that any elected government pursue the economic reforms begun by the caretakers with the blessing of the International Monetary Fund.

Sharif has promised to uphold any commitments made to the IMF, but his election promises to revive the yellow taxi scheme and build airports and motorways seem at odds with the fund's insistence that Pakistan slash its budget deficit.
Sharif stops short of endorsing a new security council set up by Leghari this month that gives the military a formal advisory role in a broad range of government affairs.
Other politicians, including Bhutto, have criticised Leghari for installing himself, rather than the prime minister, as chairman of the Council for Defence and National Security.
Sharif merely says it will be up to the new parliament to debate whether to retain the controversial body.
Pakistan remains in deep economic trouble, but many businessmen are pinning their hopes on a Sharif-led government to restore investor confidence and boost industry.
"Sharif has a pro-business image and this could help turn things around in the next few months," said an executive at a Karachi brokerage firm, who asked not to be named.
Groomed by a military ruler, Sharif first became premier in November 1990 after Bhutto's first government was sacked.
His long rivalry with Bhutto has its roots in the early 1970s when her father, former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, nationalised his father's Ittefaq Foundries.
Former military ruler General Mohammed Zia-ul-Haq picked the plump, balding Sharif as finance minister of Punjab province in 1981 and helped his family by returning their industries.

He led the PML to victory in the 1990 elections, stitching together the Islamic Democratic Alliance (IDA), an uneasy alliance of liberal groups and rightist Islamic militants, though Bhutto protested that the polls were heavily rigged.
In 1991 Sharif rammed through legislation to make the Islamic code, or Sharia, Pakistan's supreme law.
He was born in Lahore on December 25, 1949 and is married with two daughters and two sons.
